items.sentence_raw: Travelling around Thailand in the 1990s, William Janssen was impressed with the basic rooftop solar heating systems that were on many homes, where energy from the sun was absorbed by a plate and then used to heat water for domestic use.
items.explain: Q14: Section A starts with Janssen seeing solar heaters in Thailand — that was his *'initial inspiration'*. Then it says *'Two decades later Janssen developed that basic idea... into a portable device'* — this is the *'new product'*. So the heading **iii** (*'From initial inspiration to new product'*) fits perfectly.

items.sentence_raw: Two decades later Janssen developed that basic idea he saw in Southeast Asia into a portable device that uses the power from the sun to purify water.

Then it says *'Two decades later Janssen developed that basic idea... into a portable device'* — this is the *'new product'*. items.sentence_raw: The Desolenator operates as a mobile desalination unit that can take water from different places, such as the sea, rivers, boreholes and rain, and purify it for human consumption.
items.explain: Q15: Section B says the Desolenator *'can take water from different places, such as the sea, rivers, boreholes and rain, and purify it'*. This means it cleans water from many sources. So the heading **vi** (*'Cleaning water from a range of sources'*) matches exactly.

items.sentence_raw: It is particularly valuable in regions where natural groundwater reserves have been polluted, or where seawater is the only water source available.

Janssen saw that there was a need for a sustainable way to clean water in both the developing and the developed countries when he moved to the United Arab Emirates and saw large-scale water processing.
"I was confronted with the enormous carbon footprint that the Gulf nations have because of all of the desalination that they do," he says.
The Desolenator can produce 15 litres of drinking water per day, enough to sustain a family for cooking and drinking.
Its main selling point is that unlike standard desalination techniques, it doesn't require a generated power supply: just sunlight.
items.explain: Q16: Section C explains the device's main advantage: *'unlike standard desalination techniques, it doesn't require a generated power supply: just sunlight'*. This is what makes it different from other methods. So the heading **v** (*'What makes the device different from alternatives'*) is correct.

items.sentence_raw: It measures 120cm by 90 cm, and is easy to transport, thanks to its two wheels.
items.explain: Q21: The passage says the device *'is easy to transport, thanks to its two wheels'*. The question asks what helps it move to different locations. So the answer is **wheels**.

items.sentence_raw: Water enters through a pipe, and flows as a thin film between a sheet of double glazing and the surface of a solar panel, where it is heated by the sun.
items.explain: Q22: The passage describes water entering and flowing *'as a thin film'* over the solar panel. The question asks for the form of water on the panel. So the answer is **film**.

items.sentence_raw: The warm water flows into a small boiler (heated by a solar-powered battery) where it is converted to steam.
When the steam cools, it becomes distilled water.
The device has a very simple filter to trap particles, and this can easily be shaken to remove them.
items.explain: Q23: The passage says *'The device has a very simple filter to trap particles'*. The question asks where particles are caught. So the answer is **filter**.

items.sentence_raw: There are two tubes for liquid coming out: one for the waste - salt from seawater, fluoride, etc. - and another for the distilled water.
items.explain: Q24: The passage says one tube is *'for the waste - salt from seawater, fluoride, etc.'*. The question asks what comes out of the other tube. So the answer is **waste**.

items.sentence_raw: The performance of the unit is shown on an LCD screen and transmitted to the company which provides servicing when necessary.
items.explain:
Q25: The passage says *'The performance of the unit is shown on an LCD screen'*. The question asks what the screen displays. So the answer is **performance**.

Q26: The passage says the company *'provides servicing when necessary'* after seeing the data. The question asks what the device needs when the company is alerted. So the answer is **servicing**.

items.explain: Q17: Section D gives numbers: *'two-thirds of the world's population lives with severe water scarcity'* and *'half... will be living with water stress'*. These are facts about how many people lack water. So the heading **x** (*'The number of people affected by water shortages'*) is the right choice.

items.sentence_raw: "It is really important that a sustainable solution is brought to the market that is able to help these people," he says.
Many countries "don't have the money for desalination plants, which are very expensive to build.
They don't have the money to operate them, they are very maintenance intensive, and they don't have the money to buy the diesel to run the desalination plants, so it is a really bad situation."
The device is aimed at a wide variety of users - from homeowners in the developing world who do not have a constant supply of water to people living off the grid in rural parts of the US.
items.explain: Q18: Section E says the device is *'aimed at a wide variety of users'* — from homeowners in poor countries to people in rural US. This describes who might buy it. So the heading **iv** (*'The range of potential customers for the device'*) fits.

items.sentence_raw: The first commercial versions of the Desolenator are expected to be in operation in India early next year, after field tests are carried out.

The market for the self-sufficient devices in developing countries is twofold - those who cannot afford the money for the device outright and pay through microfinance, and middle-income homes that can lease their own equipment.
"People in India don't pay for a fridge outright; they pay for it over six months.
They would put the Desolenator on their roof and hook it up to their municipal supply and they would get very reliable drinking water on a daily basis," Janssen says.
In the developed world, it is aimed at niche markets where tap water is unavailable - for camping, on boats, or for the military, for instance.
Prices will vary according to where it is bought.
In the developing world, the price will depend on what deal aid organisations can negotiate.
In developed countries, it is likely to come in at $1,000 (£685) a unit, said Janssen, "We are a venture with a social mission.
items.explain: Q19: Section F quotes Janssen: *'We are a venture with a social mission'* and the product is for *'the developing world and humanitarian sector'*. This shows helping people is more important than making money. So the heading **viii** (*'Profit not the primary goal'*) is correct.

items.sentence_raw: We are aware that the product we have envisioned is mainly finding application in the developing world and humanitarian sector and that this is the way we will proceed.

items.sentence_raw: We do realise, though, that to be a viable company there is a bottom line to keep in mind," he says.
The company itself is based at Imperial College London, although Janssen, its chief executive, still lives in the UAE.
It has raised £340,000 in funding so far.
items.explain: Q20: Section G states the company *'has raised £340,000 in funding so far'*. **'Funding'** means money for the business. So the heading **i** (*'Getting the finance for production'*) matches.

items.sentence_raw: Within two years, he says, the company aims to be selling 1,000 units a month, mainly in the humanitarian field.
They are expected to be sold in areas such as Australia, northern Chile, Peru, Texas and California.
